summary.summary: Bristol's 2024/25 treasury outturn shows long-term debt rising to £600m (average rate 4.56%) against treasury investments of just £55m, lifting net debt by £118m to £545m — the first year of a five-year strategy that envisages up to £996m of new borrowing to fund the capital programme. The council remains substantially under-borrowed against its £969m capital financing requirement (CFR, the underlying need to borrow), funding the gap from cash rather than loans, and it complied with every treasury limit; general-fund financing costs were a moderate 7.18% of net revenue. Two watch items stand out: the £165m of new PWLB (Public Works Loan Board) debt was taken very short (about 1.2-year average life), so £70m — 12% of the book — matures within twelve months and must be rolled, and lenders called two LOBO loans in-year, the council repaying £35m at par rather than accept resets near 5.9%, leaving £35m of LOBOs (lender-option loans) at medium call risk.

signals.headline: Net debt up £118m to £545m and total borrowing to £600m in 2024/25 as £165m new PWLB drawn
signals.why: Debt is climbing at the start of a strategy that envisages up to £996m of new borrowing over 2024-2029.

signals.headline: £165m new PWLB (Feb-Mar 2025) taken at ~1.2yr average life; £70m (12%) of debt matures within 12 months at 31 Mar 2025
signals.why: A concentrated near-term maturity wall that must be refinanced at whatever rates prevail on maturity.

signals.headline: Lenders called LOBO options in-year: £10m Dexia (05/12/2024) and £25m Commerzbank (24/02/2025) repaid at par vs ~5.9% resets; £35m LOBOs remain at medium call risk
signals.why: A called LOBO is repaid at par, as both of these were. The remaining £35m is therefore a refinancing and liquidity exposure — cash to repay and funding to replace — not a rate-reset one.

news_drafts.headline: Bristol schools deficit stands at £87.8m after £46.7m overspend in 2025/26; £44.8m forecast this year
news_drafts.lead:
Bristol's schools funding deficit stood at £87.8m at the end of 2025/26, up from £55.9m brought forward, the Schools Forum was told on 29 September. The deficit is an overspend on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. In Bristol it sits in the "high needs" block, the part of the funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The DSG overspend in 2025/26 was £46.7m. The £87.8m carried into 2026/27 is after Safety Valve funding of £30.7m, under an agreement with the Department for Education (DfE), and council reserves, which are money set aside. The paper says the council's General Fund also holds a separate reserve under that agreement, standing at £21.9m on 31 March. At the end of June, the first quarter of 2026/27, the council was forecasting a further in-year overspend of £44.8m on the high needs block. The paper attributes it to more pupils and greater complexity of need, inflationary and funding rate increases, and additional commissioned provision.

That forecast leaves out a High Needs Stability Grant, which the DfE has proposed if the council's Local SEND Reform Plan is approved. The paper says the forecast "does not currently assume receipt" of the grant, with government confirmation of the outcome expected by the end of October.

news_drafts.headline: Bristol's schools funding deficit reached £85.4m at 31 March 2026, after a £29.5m overspend in the year
news_drafts.lead:
Bristol City Council's deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) stood at £85.4m at 31 March 2026, the draft statement of accounts (the council's formal annual accounts) shows. Of that, £29.5m was added in 2025/26. The overspend is mainly on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

The council is in the Department for Education's Safety Valve programme, which is aimed at bringing high needs spending under control. Its external auditor's interim annual report says the £85.4m is the figure after Safety Valve funding and council reserve contributions. The council has submitted a plan for reforming support for children with special needs which, if approved, would bring grant funding of up to 90% of the historic deficit. The auditor puts forecast deficits at £42.2m for 2026/27 and £25.3m for 2027/28, and describes the funding position as uncertain.

A statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, runs until 31 March 2028. After that, unless the government has taken a different approach or the deficit has been cleared, it would have to be met from the council's usable reserves (the part of its reserves it can actually spend). The auditor gives the council's general working balance as £38m, 6% of its budget. In its letter of representation to the auditor, the council also says it will report an uncorrected error in its high needs spending to the Department for Education. The letter gives no figure.

news_drafts.headline: Bristol council forecasts £0.3m overspend as advertising screens project stalls
news_drafts.lead: Bristol City Council's Economy and Skills Committee heard that a digital advertising screens project, intended to generate income for the city, has stalled and is now forecast to push the Economic Development service £0.3m into overspend. The council had budgeted £0.5m in savings this year, including £0.3m from the screens, but now forecasts to deliver only £0.25m. The project faces delays to planning permission and installation; only 70 per cent of screens are expected to be operational by September. The service is reviewing alternative options but the outcome remains uncertain. In the capital programme, Temple Meads Development is forecast to underspend by £8.4m as the project moves into a defects period; contingency funding has been moved to next year.

findings.headline: The council reports that treasury activity stayed within approved limits and that there were no breaches of its ethical investment policy in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says all treasury transactions were authorised and within approved limits, and that all investments were with counterparties on the approved lending list.
findings.matters: A finance director can use this as a benchmark for compliance reporting, and a lender can see that the council reports no treasury limit breaches for the year.
findings.figures: No breaches reported; all investments with approved counterparties
findings.quote: It should be noted that there have been no breaches during the year.

findings.headline: The Bristol Climate Action Investment raised £2m across two community municipal investment raises, at a fixed rate linked below the PWLB rate.
findings.detail: The funds are allocated to energy efficiency upgrades on council-owned assets, including solar panels, heat pumps and LED lighting. The paper describes the scheme as a diversification of funding sources.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council may consider a resident-facing municipal bond as an alternative funding source, and a lender can see a new small-scale source of funds.
findings.figures: £2m raised across two raises; rate linked below PWLB; funds applied to council-owned assets
findings.quote: During the year the Council successfully completed the two raises totalling £2m.

findings.headline: Internally managed investments averaged £113m and returned 4.10%, against a SONIA benchmark of 4.01%.
findings.detail: The paper says the council held no liquidity difficulties during the year. Investments were £50m at 31 March 2026 against £55m a year earlier.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare returns on internally held cash against the SONIA benchmark, and it shows the cash held in lieu of borrowing during the year.
findings.figures: £113m average internally managed balance (£98m in 2024/25); 4.10% average return (4.96% in 2024/25); 4.01% SONIA; £50m at 31 March 2026; £55m at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The comparable performance indicator is the Sterling Overnight Index average (SONIA), which was 4.01%

findings.headline: New PWLB borrowing averaged 4.25% for an average duration of 1 year, against a PWLB average 1-year rate of 4.52% for the year.
findings.detail: The paper uses this comparison as its debt performance indicator. The rate on the new PWLB borrowing sits below the average 1-year PWLB rate for the year.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare its own new borrowing rate against the market reference rate, and a lender can see the council's achieved borrowing cost relative to published PWLB rates.
findings.figures: 4.25% average rate on PWLB borrowing undertaken; 1 year average duration; 4.52% PWLB average 1-year rate
findings.quote: The average rate of PWLB borrowing undertaken was 4.25% with an average duration of 1 year compared to the PWLB average 1 year rate for the year of 4.52%.

findings.headline: Financing costs were 9.00% of the net revenue stream for the General Fund and 6.46% for the HRA in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper reports these as the actual financing cost indicator against net revenue stream, net of investment income. No comparison with earlier years is given in the paper.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can benchmark financing cost against its own net revenue stream, and a lender can track this ratio as a measure of debt-service burden.
